title: Project maintenance: servicing, warranties and insurance
excerpt: How a company in Moldova can distinguish servicing agreements, supplier warranties and equipment insurance assessment after project handover.
imageAlt: A technical specialist and project manager reviewing maintenance records for a modern production installation

seo.title: Project maintenance and insurance in Moldova | ING Broker
seo.description: Check handover, equipment, servicing, warranties, spare parts and interruption separately. Prepare assessment without assuming a universal maintenance policy.
seo.keywords: project maintenance insurance Moldova, equipment maintenance, servicing warranty insurance, production line maintenance, business interruption assessment

author: ING Broker editorial team
content:
Project maintenance means organising servicing and interventions after equipment or works are installed or handed over. Service agreements, supplier warranties and insurance have different roles. A company in the Republic of Moldova should read them separately and identify uncertainties between handover, operation and repairs.

This material helps project owners, building managers and technical leads prepare risk information. It does not confirm that a universal “maintenance insurance” policy exists and provides no technical work instructions. Availability and conditions require individual assessment. Equipment safety and technical work require competent specialists, not an editorial checklist.

Define the project before requesting a solution

Describe the project and its components: building, production line, installation, machine or fit-out. Record address, owner, user and current stage. A project in testing is not automatically fully handed over and established in operation. Separate accepted sections from continuing work.

Prepare a simple role map: designer, supplier, installer and maintainer. One business may have several roles, but this should not be assumed. Accurate responsibilities support useful document and risk questions without themselves establishing legal liability.

Document handover and acceptance

Collect handover records, check results and open points. Identify the installation version they describe. Record modules or components changed later. Old acceptance does not demonstrate the whole current configuration was checked at that stage.

Communicate real dates and status for insurance assessment, including unfinished testing or interventions. Do not present preliminary discussion as active protection. Request confirmation of the accepted period and operations. Handover may mean different things in works contracts, servicing and insurance, requiring separate clarification.

What does the service agreement actually promise?

Read included services: scheduled inspections, requested interventions, diagnosis, labour or parts supply. Do not add unmentioned services. “Complete service” in marketing is insufficient for planning restart. Request the list of operations and their conditions, and identify who can confirm them in writing.

Check response time separately from repair time. A technician answering a phone does not mean a part is immediately available. Record diagnosis, transport and procurement dependencies. Do not turn a supplier estimate into an ING Broker promise or insurer compensation deadline.

Consider a hypothetical company moving installation servicing to another business. Record the new provider, actual services and intended commencement. Two documents called “technical maintenance” are not necessarily identical. Compare checks, diagnosis, labour and parts separately, leaving unresolved services open.

A supplier warranty is not insurance

Keep the warranty and its use and maintenance requirements. Identify who receives fault reports and which documents they request. Do not assume every defect is repaired free or each replaced part restarts all relevant periods. Ask for explanations applying to the equipment and document.

Read the insurance contract's insured property, risks, period, limits and exclusions, meaning situations without cover. A commercial warranty establishes neither automatic inclusion nor exclusion of an incident. Keep supplier communications and separately follow the insurer's notification procedure.

What property is recorded and at which value?

Inventory important components with available identifiers and valuation documents. Separate owned items from leased, rented or partner-provided property. Record who bears the expenses discussed and the documents supporting them. An accounting total may need explanation before use in a proposal.

Separate equipment price from installation, transport, programming and other restart costs. A declared amount does not automatically include them all. Ask for valuation bases and documents for relevant categories. When replacing a component, update inventory and check whether insurance records need changing.

For an internal check, trace one important machine from the inventory to its warranty and servicing records. Explain differing identifiers instead of altering original supplier documents. This improves the file's clarity without certifying technical condition or insurance cover.

Scheduled maintenance and breakdown are different

Show planned interventions and observed deficiencies. Keep service reports, findings and recommendations. Do not erase a known alert or deferred recommendation to simplify the file. An accurate timeline is more useful than an unverifiable general description.

Do not equate wear, routine maintenance, defects and accidental damage. Ask how documents define and treat them. A list of possible technical problems is not a list of accepted policy risks. Qualified specialists establish the cause and necessary technical measures. The person organising the file does not replace their assessment.

How is work organised during intervention?

Describe full shutdown, partial shutdown or another operating configuration. Identify access coordination and applicable procedures. This article does not recommend live electrical work or dangerous operations. Do not change equipment or settings to complete an insurance sheet or photograph.

Ask about property being worked on, nearby assets and the contractor's role. Their liability policy does not automatically cover every instance of damage to a customer's installation. Request documents and conditions for actual operations. Compare the commercial agreement and proposal instead of treating their names as equivalent.

The technical team checks competence and procedures, while administration gathers contracts. Supplying installation control is not needed to demonstrate servicing. Ask whether insurance information requires updating, keeping answers with the applicable version. A response about another agreement should not transfer automatically.

Parts and alternative suppliers affect restart

Identify single-source components and long procurement periods. Separate confirmations from internal estimates. Alternative parts need specialist compatibility and consequence checks. The same price or physical fit does not establish technical or contractual acceptance.

Keep service contacts and intervention approval routes. Who requests parts, confirms orders and documents installation? Do not transmit passwords or control access for a commercial discussion. Assessment may require technical information without operational control of company equipment.

Describe interruption separately from repair costs

Show which operation stops without the equipment and available alternatives. A low-value device can block an important production stage. Record dependencies and expenditure without invented daily losses. Label planning estimates and retain their calculation documents.

If possible interruption protection is discussed, ask for the triggering event, period and calculation method. Do not assume every stoppage or service delay is accepted. Property and financial consequences may have different conditions. Check the proposal without promising full recovery of planned income.

Review recovery planning separately: confirmed contacts, purchase approvals and parts without clear lead times. Do not replace uncertainty with an optimistic immediate-repair assumption. Keep previous warnings and outstanding work rather than deleting them for a cleaner presentation. This hypothetical example separates service, warranty, safety and insurance; it is not a real customer or liability determination.

Example: maintaining a packaging line

A manufacturer prepares a line inspection. Checks and labour are contracted, but received documents do not clarify a control module's availability. This is illustrative, not a real customer. The technical lead asks the supplier while accounting separates part cost from production interruption.

The company does not treat a service response as insurance evidence. It prepares inventory, history and an interruption scenario, then asks about relevant conditions. If a new part changes configuration, records are updated after technical checking. Separate who repairs, which costs are contracted and what insurance may assess.

What to check before comparing prices

Compare the same property, activities, sites and periods. A premium is the amount paid for insurance. An excess or deductible is the portion borne by the insured under the contract. Read these alongside limits, exclusions and notification duties, not merely a product title.

Keep company requirements, answers and supporting documents in a table. An unanswered condition does not become included because it was omitted from discussion. Clarify differences between offer and schedule before deciding. Insurance ING Broker SRL acts as broker; acceptance and claims decisions belong to the insurer under the contract.

Maintenance preparation sheet

  • Project, current configuration and handover stage.
  • Components and valuation records.
  • Supplier, installer, operator and service company.
  • Maintenance contracts and commercial warranties.
  • Inspections, known deficiencies and open interventions.
  • Essential parts and procurement dependencies.
  • Interruption effects and operational alternatives.
  • Policy, notification and document questions.

Frequently asked questions about maintenance and insurance

Does servicing replace machinery insurance?

Do not regard them as equivalent. Read provider obligations separately from policy risks and conditions. A repair service alone does not establish payment for damage or interruption losses.

Can an already known fault be included?

Disclose the real situation and request document assessment. A new policy should not be assumed to resolve an existing defect or loss retrospectively. Do not conceal history to simplify a proposal.

What if I change the maintenance provider?

Update roles, services and records. Ask about conditions dependent on maintenance or interventions. Do not assume every provider and procedure is accepted identically under all contracts.

Must all technical reports be sent initially?

Start with an accurate description and request the necessary list. Send sensitive documents only through the agreed channel. Do not send system access, passwords or customer data to request general information.
